answer.rationale: At day 71 the binding constraint is the 14-day expiry with no auto-renew, and the assembly line is already at 94% of committed volume, so the decision that must be made is the primary supply contract. Switching primary vendors is ruled out because onboarding would create delivery risk at the same moment the contract lapses, violating the primary objective. Deferring is also ruled out because the contract does not auto-renew; doing nothing means supply stops. Adding a second source does not by itself resolve the imminent primary contract expiry and is therefore not the one action that best matches the time pressure. Renewing the incumbent outright preserves delivery continuity but, under an 18% spend cut, does not actively recover cost. The best single move is negotiate_terms: enter renewal negotiation now with a short, time-boxed objective of securing volume pricing, better payment terms, and price concessions against market benchmarks. Memories c4 and c1 support that renegotiating at renewal with benchmark pressure can move the incumbent on price and terms while keeping integration and deliveries stable, so this path addresses finance's cut without introducing migration or disruption risk. Memory c6 supports that longer-term commitments can unlock volume pricing without narrowing service scope, but because I have only one verification pull, I choose to verify c6 because it most directly bears on whether a multi-year term can absorb the required cost reduction; if it comes back as expected, negotiation can reasonably target the 18% cut through volume concessions rather than supplier change. If verification returns weak or contradictory support, I would fall back to renew_incumbent on a shorter term rather than switching vendors, preserving delivery stability over maximum cost reduction.
